analysis.one_liner: Bans most unsolicited telemarketing calls to consumers who join a national FTC-maintained do-not-call registry.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a floor vote and died when the 108th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Federal Trade Commission to build a do-not-call list for each state and barred telemarketers from calling numbers on it, calling at dinner hours, sending junk faxes, or using autodialers and recorded messages. It would also have barred telemarketers from hiding their caller ID, required data brokers to purge do-not-call numbers from the lists they sell, and let consumers sue violators in state court for up to $500 per call.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who want fewer sales calls at home, especially at dinner hours, plus anyone whose call-screening is circumvented by blocked caller ID. The bill also helps consumers' ability to enforce the rules themselves through small-claims style suits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Telephone consumers who want fewer sales calls

how_it_helps.text: Establishes a consumer-initiated, state-by-state do-not-call registry that telemarketers would be barred from calling, with the FTC keeping the list current quarterly and merging in state lists [S2, S3].
Bars calls between 9 p.m. and 9 a.m. and between 5 p.m. and 7 p.m., bans automated dialing and recorded messages for sales calls, and prohibits junk faxes for solicitations [S3].
Makes it unlawful to knowingly block or circumvent caller ID so consumers can screen calls [S3].

Lets consumers sue in state court to stop violations and collect actual losses or $500 per call, up to triple with attorney's fees for willful violations, and treats violations as unfair or deceptive trade practices enforceable by the FTC [S3].
Requires companies selling consumer contact lists to telemarketers to strip out anyone on the do-not-call list [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Telemarketing companies and the data brokers who sell consumer contact lists, who would lose the ability to call or sell the numbers of people who opted out, plus they would bear the cost of buying the registry and screening their call lists.

drawbacks.text: The ban exempts political campaigns, parties, and referendum groups, so some of the most intrusive calls would continue legally [S3].
It also exempts nonprofit fundraisers and lets companies keep calling existing customers they have a prior relationship with, limiting how much relief consumers would actually get [S3].

A do-not-call registry could reduce legitimate sales jobs and business volume in the telemarketing sector, and charities that rely on phone fundraising would face tighter rules even if formally exempt.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer benefit is substantial and direct—fewer intrusive calls at home, enforceable penalties, and protection against ID blocking—at a cost borne mainly by a narrow commercial industry, though the political and nonprofit exemptions blunt the bill's reach.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in September 2003, the bill never got a markup or a floor vote and expired when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 25, 2003 and read twice before being referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S1, S5].
No further action was taken after the referral; the bill advanced no further in committee and never reached the Senate floor [S5].
The bill had no cosponsors [S4], which signaled little Senate appetite to move it independently.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Telemarketing companies, list brokers, and the wider direct-marketing industry benefited from the bill's failure because they avoided new calling restrictions, enforcement exposure, and consumer lawsuits. Consumers lost the specific protections this bill would have created, though a broader national Do Not Call Registry had already been implemented that year through the FTC's rulemaking process.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral; never reported it out or scheduled it for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: Only one senator ever supported the bill on the record and no votes were ever taken, so no partisan pattern is visible.

industries.note: Would have lost the ability to call or sell the numbers of consumers who opted out, faced time-of-day and technology restrictions, and become liable to consumers in court. The bill's failure meant these firms kept their existing calling practices.

industries.industry: Consumer data brokers and list compilers
industries.note: Would have been required to purge do-not-call numbers from the contact lists they sell to telemarketers, shrinking the value of their databases.
Explicitly exempted from the definition of marketing or sales solicitation, keeping their freedom to make unsolicited calls that other telemarketers would have been barred from making.
